item.title: U.S. CISA adds Check Point and UnrealIRCd flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Check Point and UnrealIRCd flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Check Point and UnrealIRCd vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

  • CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

CVE-2026-114713 (CVSS score of 8.6) is a high-severity command injection vulnerability in UnrealIRCd, an open-source IRC server software. It affects versions from 6.0.0 up to, but not including, 6.2.7.1.

The flaw is in the labeled-response module, which fails to properly sanitize the IRCv3 label message tag when including it in server replies. An attacker can exploit this weakness to inject newlines and additional commands into server-to-server communications. On networks with at least two linked servers, even an ordinary user with no special privileges can execute commands with server-level authority. This could allow them to perform privileged IRC operations, such as disconnecting users or banning them from the network.

The UnrealIRCd maintainer confirmed that attackers were already attempting to exploit the vulnerability on the internet shortly after its disclosure. However, no specific threat group or attacker identity has been publicly identified, and there is no confirmed evidence linking the attacks to a particular campaign or financial motive. The vulnerability could be abused to gain administrative control over IRC networks, manipulate users and channels, or disrupt IRC services.

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score of 7.8) is a high-severity local privilege escalation vulnerability affecting Check Point Security Gateways and Security Management products. The flaw resides in the Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon, which runs with root privileges and listens on a local, world-writable Unix socket (/tmp/dynamic_socket) without properly authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local attacker with low privileges can exploit this weakness to execute arbitrary commands as root, gaining full control over the affected device.

Threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability in attacks against unpatched Check Point gateways. According to Check Point Research, attackers first gain initial access through the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), then leverage CVE-2026-123039 to escalate privileges to root. They subsequently deploy webshells and the TSGA backdoor, establish persistence, move laterally into internal networks, and, in some cases, deploy the destroy_v6 wiper to erase data on VMware ESXi hosts.

The campaign initially targeted Israeli organizations on October 30, 2026, with destructive attacks reported against some victims. A second wave on November 2 expanded to organizations across multiple countries and sectors.

Attribution remains uncertain. The malware shares code and infrastructure characteristics with PhiliKit, a framework previously associated with UNC5221, a China-linked threat actor. However, Check Point cautions that the evidence is insufficient to confidently attribute the entire campaign to this group. Possible explanations include collaboration with another actor or a false-flag operation.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the two vulnerabilities by November 16, 2026.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

item.title: Extortion Group Claims Theft of Nearly One Billion Expedia Traveler Records
item.description:
Russian extortion group n0n claims to have stolen nearly one billion Expedia traveler records through a compromised third-party provider.

A newly formed Russian cyber extortion group called n0n claims it has hit Expedia, the world’s second-largest online travel agency, and taken data on nearly one billion travelers. Expedia confirmed to Skift on Thursday that attackers had breached its systems through a third-party data platform provider in a supply chain attack that also affected other companies.

“Expedia Group confirmed Thursday that attackers reached its systems through a compromised third-party data platform provider, in a supply chain cyberattack that also affected multiple companies.” reported the website Skift. “Acknowledgment came after several cybersecurity sites reported this week on allegations by an extortion group known as n0n that it had stolen Expedia data. “

Expedia has not confirmed the figures reported by n0n and says its investigation is still ongoing. The company confirmed it was affected by a supply chain attack in which hackers compromised a third-party data platform provider and used its trusted access to reach several companies’ systems. Expedia says its platforms remain safe for both travelers and business partners.

The amount of data allegedly stolen is substantial. N0n claims to have obtained more than 830 million loyalty program records from 35 programs, including customer email addresses, membership IDs, and points balances.

“The alleged haul includes more than 830 million loyalty program records, 58 million traveler profiles, and over 333 million consumer account and credential records.” Forbes reports. “The hack was first reported days earlier by several cybersecurity companies, after a newly established Russian extortion group known as n0n bragged that it had stolen Expedia data.”

The group also claims to have stolen 58 million traveler profiles containing home airports and account information, 333 million consumer account records containing password-like tokens, nearly 2.5 million credit card spending records linked to hashed email addresses, 72 million consumer matching records, and 500,000 guest records containing accommodation details.

Cybersecurity firms Wiz and Sentra say the attack was carried out using a stolen vendor key from Qubole, a Google Cloud Platform partner. That access gave the attackers a trusted path into Expedia’s big data platform. N0n also claims to have taken source code through live credentials it captured the same way.

N0n emerged in mid-September and, according to SOCRadar, focuses on data theft and extortion without using ransomware. It operates with a specific pressure tactic: each victim appears on its dark web leak site only as a numbered company with a countdown timer labeled “pending exposure”, and “the group only exposes a company by name if it doesn’t pay.” The site claims 224 attacks since September.

Ransom negotiator Alex Waintraub, who is not working on the Expedia case, told Forbes that n0n’s claims appear to be a way to pressure victims into paying. He said the group’s approach is unusual because it lists victims as “Company 89” or “Company 90” without revealing their names until the countdown ends and no deal is reached. If this is how the group operates, Expedia’s decision to publicly confirm the breach is an unusual move that could weaken the hackers’ pressure tactics.

Expedia reported $14.7 billion in revenue in 2025 and operates Hotels.com, Vrbo, Travelocity, Orbitz, Hotwire, and Trivago alongside its main brand. If you have an Expedia account, a Hotels.com account or a Vrbo account, all three may draw from the same data pool.

Travelers should change the passwords for their Expedia accounts using a trusted device and avoid reusing the same passwords on other services. Although the stolen password-like tokens are hashed, attackers may still be able to crack them. The stolen loyalty program data also gives hackers access to customer email addresses and points balances, which they could use to create convincing phishing messages.

Expedia says it took steps to contain the attack as soon as it became aware of it and brought in external cybersecurity experts to investigate.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Expedia)

item.title: Data Breach at La Poste Subsidiary Maileva Affects 22 Million People in France
item.description:
A cyberattack on La Poste subsidiary Maileva exposed the names and postal addresses of 22 million people, including patients and tenants.

Maileva, a subsidiary of the La Poste group, was hit in mid-September in one of the biggest cyberattacks France has seen. La Poste confirmed it to AFP..

The stolen data includes first names, last names and postal addresses of 22 million people, which are “recipients of Maileva’s client companies.” The company confirms bank details weren’t compromiseda. The specialized sites FrenchBreaches and Cyberattaque.org had flagged the breach first.

According to Le Monde, Maileva sends documents on behalf of companies, including payslips, registered letters, invoices and shareholder meeting notices. It is part of Docaposte, a subsidiary of La Poste, and says it serves more than 70,000 users. In 2024, it sent 180 million documents. However, the 22 million people affected by the breach are not Maileva’s customers. They are the people who received documents sent through its platform.

This is important because most of these people had never heard of Maileva and had no direct relationship with the company. According to Cyberattaque.org, the affected organizations include social housing providers such as Flandre Opale Habitat and Altéal, as well as medical laboratories belonging to the Inovie group, including AXBIO, BioMedilab and Biofusion. Patients of Foch Hospital in Suresnes were also affected through one of its subcontractors.

That subcontractor is Kiwee.care, which handles friendly debt collection and medical billing, and which prints and mails through Maileva. A hacker reportedly read the content of some payment reminders. Those letters carried invoice numbers, treatment dates and amounts owed. Other Kiwee clients in healthcare may be affected as well.

Maileva already notified the CNIL, the French data protection authority, and filed a criminal complaint.

A judicial investigation is underway ,” it said. “In accordance with regulations, all affected companies have been informed of the incident by Maileva.”

It also notified every affected company. Whether those companies will now tell their own patients and tenants is a separate question.

La Poste isn’t new to cyberattacks. In December 2025, La Poste confirmed a major cyber incident knocked its information systems offline, disrupting digital banking and online services for millions of customers.

On social media, La Poste said the disruption temporarily rendered several platforms inaccessible, including its main website, mobile app, digital identity service, and the Digiposte document storage platform.

The attack temporary took down its online services, including La Banque Postale online and the mobile app, laposte.fr, Digiposte, La Poste Digital Identity, and the La Poste application.

The pro-Russian hacking group, Noname057, claimed responsibility for the cyberattack.

France has faced several major cyberattacks in recent years. In 2024, breaches at Almerys and Viamedis exposed the data of more than 33 million people, while an attack on France Travail affected another 36.8 million. In February, a hacker gained access to data from 1.2 million French bank accounts using stolen credentials belonging to a government official, according to the French Economy Ministry.

In June, Tchap, the encrypted messaging platform developed by the French government for its civil servants and made mandatory last year, was breached.

This summer, attacks targeting the tax authorities compromised data linked to nearly 700,000 people. Last week, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa also revealed that a cyberattack had cost the company around €100 million.

France remains an attractive target because of its economic importance and its political position on the war in Ukraine. The scale of the problem is growing: the French data protection authority (CNIL) recorded more than 5,600 data breaches in 2024, a 20% increase compared with the previous year. The Maileva incident is another reminder that personal data can be exposed through third-party providers that people may not even know they are using.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, La Poste)

item.title: Meta Fined €805 Million in Italy Over Facebook’s Default Photo Gallery Access
item.description:
Italy fines Meta €805 million over Facebook’s access to Android users’ photo galleries without specific consent, affecting around 20 million people.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million. The reason is that the Facebook app for Android reached into photos, videos, and their metadata on Italian users’ phones without specific consent and without telling people properly what was happening.

“The Italian Data Protection Authority (Garante) has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million. Through the Facebook app for Android devices, the company accessed photos, videos, and related metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them.” reads the Garante’s announcement.

“The measure concerns the ‘Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook’ feature, available since 2023, which, while browsing, shows users photos and videos from their phone gallery as suggestions to post.”

The feature at the center of the case suggests photos and videos from users’ phone gallery as things to post while they scroll Facebook. It has been available since 2023. The Garante opened its investigation in July 2025, after a complaint from the Bolzano Consumer Protection Centre, and backed it with its own technical analysis.

The analysis found three main problems. Facebook used a single permission to access the phone’s photo gallery for several different purposes. The notice shown to users was unclear and did not explain that granting permission would also enable photo suggestions. On top of that, the feature was enabled by default.

This is important because, once users grant full access, the app can continuously read all the photos and videos stored on their devices. Neither users nor the Garante can see exactly which data the app accesses or uses.

“The checks revealed that:

  • access to the gallery is requested through a single permission, valid for the entire app and for several functions serving different purposes;
  • the authorisation is preceded by a generic notice (“enable other features”) that does not allow users to understand that they are also authorising gallery suggestions;
  • furthermore, the feature was enabled by default.” continues the statement.

Meta told Reuters users must grant device-level permission to enable the feature and can revoke it at any time through their settings.

“This is a simple feature ​that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook. ​Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and ‌they ⁠can change that permission at any time in their settings,” the company spokesperson said in a statement

The Garante pointed to Article 122 of Italy’s Privacy Code, which carries the EU’s ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats the smartphone as part of a person’s private sphere, so any access to what’s on it needs free and informed consent.

Meta argued that the Irish authority should have handled the case. The Garante said no, since the ePrivacy rules don’t include the one-stop-shop mechanism. The case also doesn’t cover whether Meta used any content to train artificial intelligence, which the company denies. The Garante did keep the option open to look separately at a new feature launched in 2026 that processes gallery content in the cloud.

Meta now has 60 days to fix things. It has to ask for consent through a separate, specific request, and explain what the feature does, that it involves gallery access, and how to turn it off. It also has to keep the feature off by default, even for people who already said yes. If Meta misses the deadline, it can’t activate the feature for anyone without valid consent.

The company also owes the Garante two reports. One is due within 30 days, on what it has started doing, and another within 90 days, on the measures it has adopted.

Several factors led to the high fine. Around 20 million Android users in Italy were affected, and the violation is still ongoing for users who have not updated the app. Meta had also been fined by the Garante in 2019 and provided only limited cooperation during the investigation.

One factor worked in Meta’s favor: the company changed the feature after the complaint. However, the Garante said these changes came too late and only applied to users who updated the app.

The fine represents about 0.47% of Meta’s global revenue. It is unlikely to cause serious financial problems for the company, but it may help give users more control over their photo privacy.


Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Meta)

item.title: The Microsoft Outage Left 15 Hotel Guests Poisoned by Chlorine
item.description:
A Microsoft 365 outage stopped a hotel’s email chlorine alert in Germany, and 15 guests were poisoned.

A hotel in Germany had a maintenance safety system for its sauna area. If the chlorine level got too high, the system emailed the operators. When Microsoft’s cloud services failed, those emails couldn’t go out, the chlorine rose, and 15 guests were poisoned, according to Notebookcheck report.

“Over a dozen guests at a theme park hotel in Germany were injured by excessive chlorine levels.” states Notebookcheck. “According to local media reports, the incident was caused by a problem with the email-based system used to control chlorine dosing, which was affected by the Microsoft outage.”

German emergency services sent 40 first responders. Local media reported that four victims were taken to hospital, and one stayed for further observation. An alarm that depends on email works until the email doesn’t.

“Guests at the Hotel Ling Bao in Phantasialand, Brühl, were injured as a result. They complained of health problems after visiting the pool. The pool was temporarily closed but has since been reopened, as the fire department informed WDR on Saturday.” states WDR. “Due to complaints from hotel guests, emergency services and the fire department were called. Thirteen guests complained of respiratory irritation; ultimately, the number of affected individuals rose to a total of 15.”

The incident shows the danger of relying on email for critical safety alerts. When the email service fails, the warning system fails too.

The trigger was a global Microsoft outage from 12 to 14 November that hit Outlook and other services. Some Japanese workers went back to fax machines to keep their businesses running. The outage wasn’t as big as the CrowdStrike failure in 2024, which disrupted a huge number of corporate computers, but this one hurt people. Tom’s Hardware notes it could have ended in something worse if the problem hadn’t been caught earlier.

This incident is a warning for anyone who relies on online services or connected devices to manage safety systems. An alarm that depends entirely on the internet can fail when the connection or cloud service goes down. In this case, the hotel had only one way to send warnings, and that system stopped working.

The solution is to have a physical or offline backup that continues to work even when internet services are unavailable. Staff must also know how to use it and practice regularly.

“This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety.” states Tom’ss Hardware. “Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline.”

A backup that nobody knows how to operate is useless. Another option is to run the servers and automation locally, rather than relying on cloud services. However, this requires more work to build and maintain, and it does not protect against local problems such as power outages.

The incident also shows how much business now depends on a few large companies. Microsoft, Google and AWS can offer reliable service at lower cost than smaller rivals or an in-house setup. When one of them goes down, millions of businesses feel it, and economic activity can stall.

For safety systems, the advice is short: architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Microsoft Outage)

item.title: SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA Target Telecom Networks to Spy on Subscribers
item.description:
Researchers uncover two threat groups, SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA, exploiting mobile networks to spy on users and intercept calls and text messages.

Telecom security firm Enea published research on two threat actors, dubbed SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA, working inside mobile networks. According to the experts, SilentAir has compromised operators since before 2025; however, a link between the two APT groups is possible and unconfirmed.

“Sophisticated threat actors are compromising Mobile Network Operators to steal information and launch attacks on other operators and their subscribers.” reads the report published by Enea. “Enea detected ongoing activity in 2026 by LIMINAL PANDA, a threat actor previously identified. We also uncovered SilentAir, a newly identified actor compromising operators since before 2025. Links between the two are possible but unconfirmed.”

Mobile networks need to communicate with each other to support roaming, calls, text messages and mobile data. They exchange this information through signalling protocols, much of it over a shared IP network called IPX. This system allows operators to work together, but attackers can also abuse the trust between them to access mobile networks.

Security problems involving SS7 were reported in 2014, followed by attacks exploiting the Diameter protocol. More recently, researchers have also identified attacks targeting GTP, another protocol used by mobile networks. This is particularly relevant because the GTPDoor malware uses it to communicate secretly with attackers.

GTPDoor is a Unix-based malware that uses the GTP-C protocol to receive hidden commands from attackers. HaxRob first analyzed it in February 2024. Palo Alto Networks later linked it to a threat cluster tracked as CL-STA-0969, which shares many characteristics with a group known as LIMINAL PANDA, tracked by CrowdStrike. In 2024, CrowdStrike assessed with low confidence that the group had links to China. Brandefence later reported with moderate confidence that some members may work for a regional office of China’s Ministry of State Security. In July 2026, POST Luxembourg reported the first detection of GTP-C attacks involving this malware.

Enea says its GTP firewall caught GTPDoor and related activity at several customers from the first quarter of 2026, and blocked it. It saw several hundred attempted covert sessions. It has directly seen or strongly suspects 5 to 10 infected operators, and believes there may be several dozen worldwide, mostly in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

The sessions carried commands to start and stop data tunnels, move sideways inside the operator, launch SSH, check the malware’s health and hide traces by deleting files and altering timestamps. Early in an infection the attackers tried to open tunnels often, and later the gaps grew. Half the tunnels lasted under 21 minutes, and a few ran over 24 hours. That doesn’t match the daily scheduled script CrowdStrike described.

LIMINAL PANDA has developed a new version of its malware, called GTPDoor v3. This version hides in GTP-U, the part of the protocol used to carry data. This makes it harder to detect because GTP-U traffic is more complex, carries much more data than GTP-C, and receives less security attention. The malware still uses the same XOR key, but now relies on libpcap to capture network traffic. This method is less visible to standard system tools such as netstat and lsof. Another important difference is that GTP-U is also used in 5G networks, while GTP-C is not.

SilentAir uses a different approach. Enea assesses with high confidence that the group is a state-level actor rather than a commercial surveillance provider. However, the researchers have only low confidence that it is linked to China. SilentAir launches SS7 and Diameter attacks from compromised network nodes inside mobile operators in at least six Asian countries. Its operations target subscribers in around a dozen other countries and territories. Taiwan is the main target, including political figures and government officials.

The attack mix gives it away. Interception makes up 18.30% of SilentAir’s activity, against 2.07% for typical surveillance firms. Those firms favor information harvesting (61.89%) and location tracking (30.90%), while SilentAir does 7.21% and 0.22%. The attacks come in bursts, from a handful of subscribers up to several thousand in a month, then go quiet for months.

For interception, the attacker moves a target’s registered location to a node it controls, so later calls and texts pass through it. Enea saw two-factor codes arrive right after interception for some targets, which suggests the goal is to break into their other accounts. Unlike the Russian-linked HiddenArt, SilentAir really runs the compromised nodes and answers transactions it started. Enea couldn’t analyze the binary because the operators kept tight discipline.

Silent SMS, which shows no alert on the phone, is the odd part. Most go to Taiwanese subscribers around midnight, and they probably test whether interception is still working, since phones are least likely to re-register then. They’re sent through a middleman SMS center and carry cheerful spam like health wishes, in case a carrier strips the silent flag and the message appears. Nobody should be suspicious of a stranger wishing them a strong body and a calm mind, which is exactly the idea.

The China-nexus judgment rests on state-level behavior, the Taiwan focus, no targeting of Chinese networks, and activity that fits a UTC+8 workday. There are dips in the morning and evening, pauses around Chinese holidays and essentially nothing on weekends, and the targets include political VIPs. Enea rates this low confidence, so treat it as a lead, not a verdict.

Enea couldn’t confirm a link to LIMINAL PANDA. Timing sometimes overlaps in the same operators, and the targeting matches, and a trojan called SCTPE tied to LIMINAL PANDA sends SS7 and Diameter traffic. But SilentAir answers transactions SCTPE can’t handle, its operational security looks better, and its working hours differ slightly. Two China-nexus actors sharing access, or both having compromised the same operators, are equally possible.

Enea says it helped customers remove LIMINAL PANDA activity, contacted other affected operators and warned those infected by SilentAir about malicious activity in their networks. Both groups have been stopped for now. Enea warns that access to one of the world’s 800-plus mobile operators can provide a way into others through IPX. AI also makes it easier to create new malware.

Enea recommends using GTP-C and GTP-U firewalls that share information with SS7 and Diameter security tools. Operators should go beyond industry checklists and monitor internal network traffic, where tools such as SIGTRANslator and Cordscan can go unnoticed. They should also connect telecom security with regular IT security. Outsourcing core network services can make investigations more difficult.

“The IPX interface must be regarded as untrusted. The evolution of signalling security has been based on the gradual realisation that the interconnect between mobile operators cannot be regarded as a trusted link.” concludes the report. “SilentAir and in particular LIMINAL PANDA exploits any available interconnect protocol, not just SS7, Diameter, GTP, but also other protocols like DNS, ICMP etc.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, China)

Nobody should be suspicious of a stranger wishing them a strong body and a calm mind, which is exactly the idea.

The China-nexus judgment rests on state-level behavior, the Taiwan focus, no targeting of Chinese networks, and activity that fits a UTC+8 workday. There are dips in the morning and evening, pauses around Chinese holidays and essentially nothing on weekends, and the targets include political VIPs. Enea rates this low confidence, so treat it as a lead, not a verdict.

Enea couldn’t confirm a link to LIMINAL PANDA. Timing sometimes overlaps in the same operators, and the targeting matches, and a trojan called SCTPE tied to LIMINAL PANDA sends SS7 and Diameter traffic. But SilentAir answers transactions SCTPE can’t handle, its operational security looks better, and its working hours differ slightly. Two China-nexus actors sharing access, or both having compromised the same operators, are equally possible.

Enea says it helped customers remove LIMINAL PANDA activity, contacted other affected operators and warned those infected by SilentAir about malicious activity in their networks. Both groups have been stopped for now. Enea warns that access to one of the world’s 800-plus mobile operators can provide a way into others through IPX. AI also makes it easier to create new malware.

Enea recommends using GTP-C and GTP-U firewalls that share information with SS7 and Diameter security tools. Operators should go beyond industry checklists and monitor internal network traffic, where tools such as SIGTRANslator and Cordscan can go unnoticed. They should also connect telecom security with regular IT security. Outsourcing core network services can make investigations more difficult.

“The IPX interface must be regarded as untrusted. The evolution of signalling security has been based on the gradual realisation that the interconnect between mobile operators cannot be regarded as a trusted link.” concludes the report. “SilentAir and in particular LIMINAL PANDA exploits any available interconnect protocol, not just SS7, Diameter, GTP, but also other protocols like DNS, ICMP etc.”

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, China)

item.title: German Military Grounds Quantum Systems Drones Following Reported Cyberattack
item.description:
German drone maker Quantum Systems confirms a cyberattack that disrupted operations, with reports pointing to a malicious software update.

Quantum Systems, a German defense company that builds reconnaissance and interceptor drones and the software that controls them, confirmed an incident in late October.

The company says its security teams quickly contained the threat while working with government authorities. It also points out that the incident does not pose a risk to customers or operators using its drones.

The company reported the incident to the relevant authorities, and an investigation is still underway with the help of internal and external cybersecurity experts.

“Quantum Systems identified a cybersecurity incident at the end of October 2026. An immediate internal investigation revealed an active cyberattack by hostile actors. The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities.” reads the company’s statement on cyber incident. “Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems’ unmanned systems for the end users and the operators.”

The manufacturer did not disclose details technical details about the security incident.

Quantum Systems added that European defense companies have faced ongoing cyberattacks for years, particularly those supporting Ukraine. It believes this support makes them attractive targets and says it has security measures in place to protect its systems and data.

“The European defence industry has been facing persistent cyberattacks for years. Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers’ security.” concludes the statement. “Being aware of this responsibility, Quantum Systems has mitigation plans in place and strives to fulfill the highest standard of data and system security.”

According to Der Spiegel and the Financial Times, citing internal sources, attackers may have used a malicious update file for QBase, Quantum Systems’ software for controlling drones and planning missions. This suggests that the attackers may have compromised the company’s update server in a supply chain attack. The incident is particularly significant because compromising the software distribution mechanism of a drone manufacturer can potentially affect the systems used by military and other customers, even without directly compromising the drones themselves.

Der Spiegel also reports that QBase is used to plan missions for the Vector reconnaissance drone, known as Falke in the German military.

QBase is Quantum Systems’ ground-control and mission-planning software for its unmanned aerial vehicles (drones). It runs on Windows computers and is used by drone operators to plan, execute, monitor and analyze missions. QBase is not simply an application for viewing drone footage. It is part of the operational infrastructure used to prepare and manage drone missions.

An unexpected software update reached customers and raised alarms inside the company. It is not clear how many customers installed it. Reports also say that the German military grounded Quantum Systems drones as a precaution and excluded them from a recent exercise. Military counterintelligence (MAD), Germany’s domestic intelligence service (BfV), and the federal cybersecurity agency (BSI) are reportedly investigating the incident.

However, these details have not been officially confirmed, and no attacker has been identified.

The incident highlights a major security risk for companies supplying software to defense and industrial customers: attackers can target not only the products themselves but also the systems used to distribute software updates. If hackers compromise an update server, they may be able to deliver malicious files to customers who trust the vendor and install its updates.

For this reason, companies must protect their software distribution infrastructure as carefully as their production systems. They should digitally sign updates, verify their integrity before installation, restrict access to update servers and monitor any unusual activity. Customers should also be able to independently verify updates before deploying them.

Another important measure is to have a way to quickly stop or roll back an update if suspicious activity is detected. In critical environments, such as military operations and industrial control systems, a compromised update can have consequences that go far beyond data theft, potentially disrupting equipment, operations and essential services.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Systems Drones)
